alphabet.name: ka
alphabet.sound: k at the start, g in the middle
alphabet.note: Tamil has no separate letters for k and g, or p and b. The SAME letter is read hard at the start of a word and soft between vowels — so ka becomes ga in the middle. This is why Tamil needs so few consonants.

alphabet.name: cha
alphabet.sound: ch at the start, s in the middle

alphabet.name: ta
alphabet.sound: t with the tongue curled back

alphabet.name: tha
alphabet.sound: th with the tongue on the teeth

alphabet.name: pa
alphabet.sound: p at the start, b in the middle

alphabet.name: na
alphabet.sound: n with the tongue on the teeth

alphabet.name: zha
alphabet.sound: no English equivalent — tongue curled far back
alphabet.note: The sound Tamil is proudest of. It is in the word தமிழ் (Tamil) itself, which is why speakers sometimes say the language is named after a sound no one else has.

alphabet.name: la
alphabet.sound: l with the tongue curled back

alphabet.name: tra
alphabet.sound: a hard trilled r, or 'tr' when doubled

alphabet.name: na
alphabet.sound: n with the tongue curled back

alphabet.name: na
alphabet.sound: a third n — the everyday one at the end of words
alphabet.note: Tamil has three letters for n and they are not interchangeable in spelling, even where they sound close.

vocab.note: Like Malayalam, Tamil avoids a bare 'goodbye'. You say you'll go and come back.
Tamil marks respect with the plural, exactly as Malayalam does. 'Nee' to a friend, 'neenga' to anyone older.
Used for your older brother and for any man a little older — the shopkeeper, the driver. Calling him by name alone marks you as an outsider.

examples.translation: My younger brother is at school
What is the price of this?
I need to see a doctor
I want to, but I have no money
I didn't come because I was unwell
